One
wun
adj., n.
Old English an; the cardinal of unity. In Scripture the number of God’s own oneness (echad) and of the union He makes—of husband and wife, and of Christ and His body.

Biblical Definition

One is the number of God. The great confession of Israel, the Shema, declares “the LORD our God, the LORD is one”—not a solitary monad but the one living and true God who eternally subsists in three Persons, undivided in essence. From this oneness flows every biblical unity. God makes of husband and wife “one flesh,” a covenant union that images His own faithfulness. Christ prays that His people “may be one, as We are one,” and the apostle grounds the church’s unity in it: “one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.” One is therefore never the number of proud isolation but of covenant communion—a unity given by God, not manufactured by men. It rebukes both the idolatry of the many gods and the individualism that would live to itself. To confess one God is to be bound into one people; the number that begins all counting is the number that gathers the redeemed into one.

Webster 1828 Definition

The number of unity: first, the oneness of the one true God; then the covenant unions He creates—one flesh in marriage, one body in the church.

expand to see more

ONE, adj. Single in number; the first of the cardinals. In Scripture pre-eminently the number of God’s essential oneness, confessed in the Shema and never at odds with the Tri-unity of Persons.

ONE, n. The unity God creates and commands: the one-flesh bond of marriage, the one body of the church, the one faith once delivered. Biblical oneness is covenantal communion, not the lonely self-sufficiency the modern age prizes.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 6:4 — ""Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one!"

Genesis 2:24 — "Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."

John 17:21 — "that they all may be one, just as You, Father, are in Me, and I in You. May they also be in Us — so that the world may believe that You sent Me."

Ephesians 4:4 — "There is one body, and one Spirit — just as you also were called in one hope of your calling;"

Modern Corruption

Modernity keeps the word one but empties it of covenant—turning it into the autonomous individual (“be your one true self”) rather than the God-given union of the Shema and the one-flesh bond.

expand to see more

The reigning corruption is individualism: the “number one” as the sovereign self, looking out for itself, answerable to no one. Scripture’s one is the opposite—the one God who binds His people into one body, and the one flesh that dies to self for the sake of the other.

A subtler corruption dissolves oneness into a vague spiritual “all is one” (monism), erasing the Creator-creature distinction. The Shema resists both errors: God is one, and He is other than His creation, calling a distinct people into covenant union with Himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Old English an and the Hebrew echad—a oneness that can embrace plurality (one flesh from two, one God in three Persons) without ceasing to be one.

expand to see more

Old English an — single, the first cardinal.

Hebrew echad — one; a unity that can comprehend plurality (Genesis 2:24, ‘one flesh’).

Hebrew yachid — the only, solitary one; notably NOT the word chosen for God in the Shema.

Greek heis — one; Paul’s drumbeat in Ephesians 4: one body, one Spirit, one Lord.

Usage

"The Shema’s “the LORD is one” is the ground of all monotheism and the death of every idol."

"In making the two “one flesh,” God stamps marriage with His own covenant faithfulness."

"Christ’s prayer that we be one is not a call to bland uniformity but to Spirit-wrought communion."
